intro: This unit reads two kinds of biblical poetry close up. The first is the poetry of the prophets: Amos at a northern shrine, Hosea in a broken marriage, Isaiah before an Assyrian army, Jeremiah at the temple gate, Ezekiel in a valley of bones. These books speak to kings and crowds about the poor, about trust, and about what comes after disaster. Their words have traveled far: a line of Amos was quoted from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial in 1963.

The second is the poetry of the wisdom books, where the questions turn inward. Job, ruined for no reason he can see, demands a hearing from God and gets a storm. Ecclesiastes tests every path to meaning and calls it all hevel, breath. Proverbs, beside them, says that wisdom usually works. These books disagree with each other in public, inside the same Bible.

By the end of the unit you will be able to name the forms the prophets use, place each prophet in his crisis, explain how Jewish and Christian readers read the Servant Songs and the new covenant differently, describe the architecture of Job, and say what Ecclesiastes means by hevel. You will also be able to show how modern writers, from Martin Luther King Jr. to Elie Wiesel, have picked these texts up and used them.
bigQuestion: How do the prophets and the wisdom books speak to injustice and suffering, and why have readers kept returning to them?

Isaiah of Jerusalem is called in the year King Uzziah died

Sennacherib besieges Jerusalem; the city is not taken
Jeremiah is called in the thirteenth year of King Josiah
Ezekiel sees his first vision among the exiles by the river Chebar
Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple; Judah goes into exile
Cyrus of Persia takes Babylon; Isaiah 40-55 speaks comfort to the exiles

MacLeish's J.B. opens on Broadway; Pulitzer Prize the next year
King quotes Amos 5:24 in Birmingham and at the March on Washington

test.q: Amos told the worshippers at Bethel that their feasts and songs were rejected because of what?
test.why: Amos 5 rejects the offerings and demands justice like a rolling river.

test.q: Hosea 6:6 says God desires what more than burnt offerings?
choices: Steadfast love and knowledge of God
test.why: The verse ranks hesed and knowledge of God above sacrifice; Matthew reports Jesus quoting it.
God summons the mountains as witnesses and states a case, the covenant lawsuit form.

choices: Sennacherib's siege of Jerusalem in 701 BCE
test.why: Isaiah 36-37 tells of the Assyrian siege, which Assyrian records also describe from their side.

test.q: Why do most scholars read Isaiah 40-55 as coming from the exile?
choices: Its setting is Babylon after Jerusalem's fall and it names Cyrus
test.why: The changed setting and the naming of Cyrus (539 BCE) point to the exile; traditional readers hold the whole book is Isaiah's.

test.q: Which verse do Jewish readers point to when they read the servant as Israel?
test.why: Isaiah 49:3 names the servant Israel; Christian readers point instead to the singular sufferer of chapter 53.

test.q: What does the new covenant of Jeremiah 31 promise?
choices: The law written on the heart and sins forgiven
test.why: Jeremiah 31:33-34 promises the law within, on the heart, and forgiveness; Hebrews quotes it in full.

test.q: Ezekiel 37 explains the valley of dry bones as which of these?
test.why: Ezekiel 37:11 says the bones are the whole house of Israel, to be brought back to their land.

test.q: Which prophet did Martin Luther King Jr. call an extremist for justice in the Letter from Birmingham Jail?
test.why: King cited Amos's call to let justice roll down like waters.

test.q: In the book of Job, who is ha-satan in the prose opening?
choices: The adversary, a figure in the heavenly court
test.why: Ha-satan, the adversary, questions whether Job serves God for nothing; the text does not present him as Job's friend or family.

test.q: What does God say about Job's friends in Job 42:7?
choices: They should replace Job as priests
They did not speak rightly about God, as Job did
They will be given Job's wealth
test.why: The epilogue rebukes the friends and names Job as the one who spoke rightly.

test.q: Ecclesiastes' key word hevel is best translated literally as which of these?
test.why: Hevel is breath or mist; vanity and meaningless are interpretations.

test.q: Ecclesiastes is read aloud in the synagogue during which festival?
test.why: Ecclesiastes is the festival scroll for Sukkot, the fall harvest festival.

test.q: How does Proverbs differ from Job and Ecclesiastes?
choices: Proverbs is confident that wisdom usually leads to a good life; the other two test the exceptions
test.why: Scholars speak of a debate within wisdom: Proverbs states the rule and Job and Ecclesiastes press on hard cases.

test.q: Which modern writer staged a trial with God as defendant after a massacre, in a play from 1979?
test.why: Wiesel's The Trial of God (1979) is set in 1649 and grew from something he saw in Auschwitz.

write.prompt: Does the Bible let a person argue with God? Cite two or three passages from this unit (for example Jeremiah 20:7-9, Job 31:35-37, Ecclesiastes 7:15, or Jeremiah 12:1) and explain what each text says and how Jewish and Christian readers have understood the argument.
tips: Name each text you cite by book, chapter and verse before you explain it.
Attribute every belief: say who reads the text this way, not that the text simply is this.
Where Jewish and Christian readers differ, present both readings and compare them rather than judging.
Use the unit's terms: oracle, lawsuit, retribution, hevel, theodicy.
Keep sentences short and say one thing at a time.
